accepted.name: channel2_line_spend
accepted.description: The spend on this purchase line attributed to sales channel 2 (71.7% of lines), and zero for channel-1 lines. Summed over a customer's history it is that customer's channel-2 revenue; together with the channel-1 counterpart it decomposes total spend by channel, which a plain sum of price cannot do. Channel semantics (store vs online) are not recoverable from this database, so the name stays agnostic.
accepted.units: scaled price units (x590 gives the retail currency amount)
accepted.why_it_matters: Channel mix is a first-order churn covariate in retail: a customer whose revenue sits entirely in one channel behaves differently from a mixed-channel one. Price alone is channel-blind and sales_channel_id alone is amount-blind.

accepted.name: channel1_line_spend
accepted.description: The complement of channel2_line_spend: spend on this line if it went through sales channel 1 (28.3% of lines), else zero. The pair is a revenue decomposition, not a duplicate of either input; their aggregated ratio is the customer's channel-revenue share.
accepted.units: scaled price units (x590 gives the retail currency amount)
accepted.why_it_matters: Gives the minority-channel half of the spend split, so a model can form channel-revenue share by aggregation. Minority-channel-only buyers are a distinct, typically higher-churn segment.

accepted.name: premium_price_surplus
accepted.description: How far above the catalogue median unit price (0.02541 scaled, 14.99 in currency) this line sits; zero for every line at or below the median. Not a rescaling of price: it is a one-sided hinge, so it is flat over the whole bottom half of the price distribution and only measures the premium tail. Summed over a customer it is their trade-up surplus; averaged it is how far above mainstream they shop.
accepted.units: scaled price units above the median line (x590 for currency)
accepted.why_it_matters: Trade-up versus mainstream shopping separates committed customers from the price-led tail, and a linear price feature cannot express the asymmetry: the same mean price can come from all-mid-market or from a barbell of bargains plus a few premium items.

accepted.name: bargain_depth
accepted.description: How far below the lower-quartile unit price (0.016932 scaled, 9.99 in currency) this line sits, and zero for the upper three quarters of lines. The downward mirror of premium_price_surplus, deliberately a separate quantity rather than its negation because the hinge discards the other side. Aggregated, it measures spend concentrated in the bargain bin. Roughly 75% of rows should be exactly zero and the non-zero values are tightly bounded, since the cheapest line in the database is 0.000169.
accepted.units: scaled price units below the Q1 price point (x590 for currency)
accepted.why_it_matters: Discount-only shoppers are the canonical churn-prone cohort in fashion retail; they are invisible in mean price (which they share with a mixed shopper) but obvious in depth-below-Q1 once aggregated.

accepted.name: premium_channel2_line
accepted.description: Indicator that this line is both a channel-2 purchase and above the upper-quartile unit price (0.033881 scaled, 19.99 in currency), i.e. a high-value purchase in the dominant channel. Aggregated it is a count, which is information neither channel2_line_spend (an amount) nor premium_price_surplus (channel-blind) yields after summation. The exact rate depends on the joint distribution of channel and price, which these tools do not expose, so I expect a minority of rows to fire -- plausibly 10-25%.
accepted.units: indicator (0 or 1); counts lines once aggregated
accepted.why_it_matters: A count of high-value purchases in a specific channel is the frequency leg of an RFM description, conditioned on where the money was spent -- the combination of 'how often' and 'how big' and 'where' that churn models actually want.

accepted.name: contact_flags_set
accepted.description: How many of the two account flags, FN and Active, are set (0, 1 or 2). Both columns are set-or-missing: the only non-null value either takes is 1.0, with FN set on 34.8% of accounts and Active on 33.8%. The comparison is the point -- it reads null as absent, which is the correct semantics, whereas a mean-imputed or embedded null destroys the signal. The two flags are near-duplicates of each other by marginal count but not identical, so the sum is an engagement depth, not a rescaling of either. Expect roughly two thirds of accounts at 0.
accepted.why_it_matters: A marketing/activity engagement depth on the only table that describes the customer. customer has no signup date and no behavioural column, so these flags plus age are the whole cold-start profile, and the flag count is the one ordered quantity they can form.

accepted.name: subscribed_not_active
accepted.description: Indicator for the account that carries the FN flag (most likely a fashion-news opt-in, which matches the 478,258 Regularly/Monthly subscribers to within 1,328 rows) but NOT the Active flag: still on the mailing list, no longer marked active. The two flags overlap heavily, so the marginals bound this at no more than 34.8% of accounts and the true rate is likely far smaller; I cannot measure the joint with these tools.
accepted.why_it_matters: Names the directional half of the flag disagreement that points at churn -- subscribed but inactive is a lapsing account, while the reverse is a new or quiet one. contact_flags_set scores both identically at 1, so this is not recoverable from it.

accepted.name: age_deviation_from_median
accepted.description: Absolute distance in years from the median customer age of 32. Age spans every integer from 16 to 99 (hard floor and ceiling, 1.16% null), with p25 24 and p75 49, so the distribution is young-skewed with a long upper tail; the folded distance is around 8-12 for a typical customer and reaches 67 at the 99-year ceiling. Deliberately non-monotone in age, so it is not a rescaling: a 20-year-old and a 44-year-old receive the same value.
accepted.why_it_matters: Retention is U-shaped in age -- the youngest fast-fashion cohort and the oldest tail both churn more than the core -- and a linear age feature cannot represent a U. Age is the only continuous attribute customer has, so making its shape expressible matters more here than it would on a richer entity table.

accepted.name: taxonomy_sentinel_count
accepted.description: How many of the article's five coded taxonomy attributes carry the -1 unknown sentinel rather than a real code: product_type_no (121 rows), graphical_appearance_no (52), colour_group_code (28), perceived_colour_value_id (28), perceived_colour_master_id (685). Negativity is the sentinel test -- none of these taxonomies has a legitimate negative code -- so the count is an incompleteness score, 0 to 5. It is genuinely sparse: at most ~0.8% of the 105,542 articles score above zero and the mean should be near 0.001, with the 28 doubly-missing colour rows reaching 3.
accepted.why_it_matters: Collapses five sentinel conventions into one honest data-quality quantity, and it is the one thing on article that arithmetic can mean: every other code there is a label, so subtracting or ratioing them -- which the brute-force generator will do -- is nonsense. Incompletely catalogued articles are typically odd or newly loaded stock, a basket-composition signal rather than a strong churn driver, and I am claiming it as the former.

rejected.name: active_not_subscribed
rejected.description: The opposite segment: flagged Active but without the FN opt-in -- an account the retailer treats as live that has not taken the marketing subscription. Bounded above by Active's 33.8% set rate and, given the heavy overlap with FN, expected to fire on a small minority.
rejected.why_it_matters: Completes the flag decomposition with the opposite sign, so a model can tell 'engaged but unsubscribed' from 'subscribed but lapsed' rather than seeing one undifferentiated 'exactly one flag' bucket.
